entry.title: Who is bonded to whom?
entry.content:
The short version. My thesis is about what sits next to an electrode, and what changes when those neighbors change. Acetone and methylamine push Cu capacitance in opposite directions. Amines pull Cu out of a cathode, so about 13 ppm Cu is still found in solution at −0.75 V versus RHE. About 1 ppm Pb turns Ag from a poor amination catalyst into one that gives yields above 60%. In a separate CO₂-reduction system, a Cs⁺ ion that has lost some of its water gets closer to activated CO₂. Three posts follow those stories. This one shows how they fit together.

In this post

  1. The electrode comes with company
  2. Three stops at the interface
  3. The calculations have different jobs
  4. Reach it, keep it, restore it
  5. A few distinctions worth keeping

The electrode comes with company

Write “Cu cathode” in a methods section and it reads like a complete description. The experiments behind my thesis kept showing me that it isn’t. Two reactants changed the capacitance of the same Cu electrode in opposite directions. A cathode, which its negative potential should protect, lost copper into the electrolyte. A trace of lead, small enough to be written off as an impurity, changed the amine yield on Ag by more than a factor of ten.

Each of these turned into a question about neighbors: which molecules sit next to the metal, which atoms the metal is bonded to, and what happens when those partners change. The CO₂ work later added one more version of the same question, this time about a cation and the water around it.

I use “coordination” loosely here. It covers metal–ligand bonds, hydration shells, hydrogen bonds, and the metallic neighbors that hold a surface atom in place. These are different kinds of physics, and I do not pretend they obey one equation. Following how they change is simply a practical way to connect projects that would otherwise look unrelated.

Three stops at the interface

The series moves in a chemical order. First the environment around the electrode changes. Then the electrode itself changes. Finally, those changes in partners open a reaction route that was not there before.

Part 1 · Capacitance

Capacitance before reduction. Acetone raises Cu double-layer capacitance and methylamine lowers it. Both molecules are more polarizable than water, so the answer has to come from the interface as a whole.

Part 2 · Dissolution

When the cathode dissolves. Amines help a Cu atom swap metallic neighbors for nitrogen ligands. A cathodic potential slows the loss, but the solution chemistry still has a say.

Part 3 · Reactivity: Pb + Cs in CO2RR

Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation. Pb and Bi hydrides are candidate hydrogen shuttles for amination. In a separate CO₂-reduction system, a less hydrated Cs⁺ makes closer, chemically specific contact with the adsorbate.

Part 3 deliberately puts two different reactions side by side. Pb and Bi change their composition as they pass hydrogen along; Cs changes its hydration and its contact with CO₂. What links them is a change in coordination that produces a reactive arrangement. The two experimental systems stay separate throughout.

The calculations have different jobs

My part in all of these studies was computational. The experiments raised the puzzles and tested the explanations; my job was to build atomistic models that could say why.

No single model level could do that. Explicit water resolves how molecules are arranged at the surface. Molecular dynamics gives me configurations worth looking at. A continuum solvent stands in for the rest of the liquid without placing every molecule. Holding different states at a common electrode potential lets them exchange electrons with the same reservoir, as they would in a cell. Reaction-path calculations give the barriers for moving hydrogen.

More atoms help only when they resolve something that could change the answer. For the water response, that means molecular orientation. For Cu loss, it means kinks and ligands. For a hydride, the hydrogen donor and its transition state. For Cs, the number of waters, varied one at a time.

Even a detailed picture can leave out the number I most want. A frozen water configuration has a well-defined electronic response, but I may not know how often it occurs in the real liquid. An optimized hydride can have an easy transfer pathway, but I may not know how much of it is present at steady state. I try to keep those gaps in view, because they are usually where the next experiment should go.

Reach it, keep it, restore it

When I lay the studies side by side, the same three practical checks keep coming up. A useful configuration has to be reachable. Its key species have to stay around long enough to do something. And, for anything catalytic, they have to come back afterward.

Cu dissolution shows why reaching a new coordination environment can be bad news. An amine helps a Cu atom leave its metallic surroundings and become a soluble complex, and the electrode slowly loses material. The hydride work explores a different fate for a mobile metal species: carry hydrogen to the substrate, return to the electrode, and get recharged. Leaving the surface is a branching point. What happens next decides whether it is a loss or part of a cycle.

The Cs system works another way. A ligand-confined interface keeps the cation near the adsorbate while its water shell thins out, and losing water makes room for a closer contact. Nothing has to leave the electrode for the useful change to happen.

I find this more helpful than looking for the strongest adsorption or the largest capacitance. A productive configuration has to be accessible, survive its competition, and fit into the rest of the chemistry. Strong binding can help one of those and hurt another.

A few distinctions worth keeping

The numbers in this series answer different questions, and I try to keep each one attached to its own job.

Response and population

Capacitance tells me how charge responds to potential. Several structures can give the same trend, so it cannot tell me how often each structure occurs.

Intermediate and barrier

An uphill intermediate carries an energy cost. A transition state sets a barrier. An energy profile built only from intermediates does not give a dissolution rate.

A step and a cycle

An easy hydrogen-transfer step matters only if the donor forms, reaches the substrate, survives side reactions, and regenerates. A low barrier alone does not predict yield.

These distinctions came out of putting the thesis together, not out of a wish to hedge every sentence. Each one points at a specific missing piece: measure populations, find the missing transition state, track the mobile metal, account for the water reservoir.

The through-line is simple enough to keep in mind as the chemistry gets busier. Before I credit a material with some activity, I want to know who its neighbors are under reaction conditions. Part 1 starts with water, two solutes, and a capacitance trend that refused to follow the obvious explanation.

entry.title: Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation

link.title: Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation

entry.content:
The short version. About 1 ppm Pb takes reductive amination on Ag from almost no amine to yields above 60%. In my calculations, the preferred imine-hydrogenation barriers are 0.39 eV for PbH₄ in solution and about 0.47 eV for PbH₂ on Ag, compared with more than about 0.9 eV for the direct Ag routes I examined. Bi offers a similar round trip. In a separate CO₂-reduction study, going from five waters around Cs⁺ to one shortens its contact with a CO₂ oxygen from about 3.51 to 2.83 Å. Both stories come down to coordination changing hands. Whether the donor regenerates, and how many cations actually lose their water, are still open.

In this post

  1. A tiny impurity with a large effect
  2. Build a hydrogen donor
  3. A shuttle has to make the return trip
  4. Try another p-block passenger
  5. Give Cs a little less water
  6. Partial covalent means looking at the electrons
  7. A productive configuration needs a whole setting
~1 ppm Pbstrong experimental promotion of Ag amination
0.39 / 0.47 eVpreferred solution / surface Pb-assisted barriers
3.51 → 2.83 ÅCs–O contact, five- to one-water models, approximately

A tiny impurity with a large effect

In a Pb-free cell, Ag was a poor amination catalyst. Add about 1 ppm Pb and the amine yield went above 60%. That is a lot of influence from something that would normally be filed under impurities.

Part 2 showed coordination pulling metal into solution. Here I follow a friendlier consequence of a mobile metal: a species that carries hydrogen to the substrate. The reaction is still acetone reductive amination. The CO₂ system comes later, as a separate example of coordination creating reactivity.

The control experiments made it clear that “Ag cathode” was not the full description. A fresh membrane in an Ag–Pb cell gave about 29% amine; reusing it with a Pb anode raised that to about 64% by the fourth use. Elemental analysis found ppm amounts of Pb in the cathode compartment. Reusing membranes in a Pb-free cell with a Pt anode did not reproduce the activation, and adding Pb on purpose brought the high yields back.

The protocols matter too. The galvanostatic series gave about 63% at 1 ppm Pb, and the potentiostatic comparison at −2.94 V versus RHE gave about 61%; I keep them as separate comparisons. Rinsing an active Ag electrode and moving it into Pb-free electrolyte dropped the yield from 61% to 1.1%. That argues against a lasting activation that survives the transfer, while leaving room for a short-lived surface species under bias.

Build a hydrogen donor

I compared several possible hydrogen sources: H on Ag, water-mediated proton-coupled electron transfer, a Pb hydride on the surface, and a molecular Pb hydride in the nearby solution.

At −2 V versus RHE, the thermodynamics favor a high H coverage on Ag(111), so my starting model carries 16 surface H atoms in a (4 × 4) cell. That sets the environment for the pathways; it does not pin down the H distribution on a real polycrystalline electrode.

Moving the first H from Ag to Pb has a calculated barrier of 0.68 eV. The next step, to PbH₂, is about 0.51 eV, or about 0.48 eV when surface H is replenished. Forming the early hydrides directly from water costs more than 1 eV in the structures I examined. The early hydrides prefer to point H toward Ag, which makes supply from the metal side geometrically convenient.

Once PbH₂ forms, further H can be added from the surface or from water with barriers below about 0.5 eV. PbH₂ stays firmly attached to Ag in the structures tested, whereas PbH₄ has an unfavorable adsorption free energy at −2 V and can go into solution. Changing the hydrogen count changes where the species can do chemistry.

For PbH₄ in solution, the preferred N-first hydrogenation of the imine has an effective barrier of 0.39 eV, with a first step of 0.22 eV. Surface PbH₂ gives about 0.47 eV for its preferred N-first sequence. The direct Ag routes I examined are above about 0.9 eV at −2 V. The strong result is that Pb opens a lower-barrier route. The 0.08 eV gap between the two Pb routes is too small to say which one dominates at steady state.

A shuttle has to make the return trip

The solution-phase proposal is a PbH₄/PbH₂ shuttle. Ag charges Pb with hydrogen, PbH₄ leaves and hands two H atoms to the imine, and PbH₂ goes back to Ag to be recharged. Surface-bound PbH₂ offers an alternative in which the hydrogen transfer stays at Ag.

A good transfer barrier only gets the proposal partway home. Pb hydrides can also react with water and release H₂, with side-reaction barriers of about 0.5–0.8 eV. Even with a lower imine barrier, the competition depends on encounter rates and activities: water is everywhere, while the local imine supply depends on condensation and transport.

Flow-cell measurements coupled to ICP-MS support the idea of a mobile Pb inventory, but they do not directly detect PbH₄ in the working aqueous cell. Likewise, amine yields that barely change across the −1.34 to −3.34 V window fit a chemical step in solution once enough donor is generated, but they do not prove that step is rate-determining.

A hydride shuttle has to form, survive, find the substrate, and come back. My calculations make Pb-mediated hydrogen transfer plausible and lower in barrier than the Ag routes I examined. They leave open how the work is split between the surface and solution cycles.

Try another p-block passenger

A follow-up study asked whether the mechanism could help choose a different mediator. Several p-block additives were screened experimentally, and I calculated hydrogen transfer for AsH₃, H₂Se, InH₃, SnH₄, SbH₃, H₂Te, TlH₃, PbH₄ and BiH₃.

These are molecular models, not a census of what exists in water. The sixth-period TlH₃, PbH₄ and BiH₃ give favorable product-forming energy landscapes in the comparison, while the lighter candidates have less favorable intermediates or products. That holds for this substrate and this family of models; it is not a periodic-table rule.

For BiH₃, the barrier is 0.29 eV for N-first hydrogenation and 0.56 eV for C-first. Handing over two H atoms leaves BiH. In the proposed return route, BiH goes back to Ag, picks up hydrogen through surface chemistry to become BiH₃ again, and is released. It parallels the Pb picture without assuming that transport, adsorption or hydrolysis are the same.

At 1 ppm additive, amine yields were about 54.3% for Tl and 36.9% for Bi, against about 60.8% for the matched Pb reference; the lighter elements tested gave about 1–3%. Raising Bi to 6 ppm brought the yield to about 59.7%, with no further gain at 7 ppm. Similar yields at different loadings do not mean similar turnover frequencies.

Deep dive: why transfer energetics cannot rank the full mediators

A transition state has to be referenced to the intermediate before it, especially if that intermediate sits well below the starting reactants. A full comparison also needs donor formation and regeneration. In the Bi concentration series, yield rises while turnover number per added Bi falls, and carbon balances are roughly 70–75%. None of these measurements gives the fraction of Bi present as active BiH₃. At 6 ppm Bi and 25 °C, Pt and Ni gave yields below 10%, a reminder that the electrode still matters for making the proposed molecular donor.

Give Cs a little less water

The CO₂ study starts from a different problem. At a ligand-confined Ag interface, how does a shortage of water change what Cs⁺ can do for a CO₂-derived adsorbate? My part was the electronic-structure and interface modeling.

The catalyst is a nanoparticle-ordered ligand interlayer, or NOLI. Conditioning Ag nanoparticles capped with tetradecylphosphonic acid detaches ligands, which then stay close to the aggregated particles. The space between them holds water and ions but is not bulk electrolyte. The question is whether losing part of its hydration lets Cs⁺ make a closer, chemically specific contact with an oxygen of CO₂.

I compared seven constructed states, from a remote six-water Cs⁺ to progressively less hydrated configurations near Ag(111). With the remote reference, CO₂ stays nearly linear at 179.9°, with an average Cs–O distance of about 4.56 Å. Just bringing the six-water environment closer bends CO₂ to about 171.0°.

Across the five- to one-water models near the surface, the Cs–O distance falls from about 3.51 to 2.83 Å, and the CO₂–Ag distance from about 2.82 to 2.19 Å. The Cs–O ICOHP values go from about −0.11 through −0.14, −0.18 and −0.19 to −0.20 eV. Within this family of models, less water goes with a closer approach and more net bonding.

The “nearly bare” cation in the title is still damp: even the least hydrated state keeps one explicit water. Partial desolvation is the mechanism being tested.

Partial covalent means looking at the electrons

A shorter distance alone does not tell me what kind of bond it is. I looked at orbital overlap, charge-density differences, electron localization, Bader charges and crystal orbital Hamilton populations. Together they support a partial covalent contribution on top of a substantial electrostatic interaction.

Cs⁺ is still an alkali-metal cation. Partial covalent character means the Cs–O contact has a chemically specific electronic component. It does not assign an integer bond order or take away the ionic character.

Reference crystals help calibrate the diagnostics. CsI, CsHCO₃ and Cs₂CO₃ put the same element in different anion environments. For selected short contacts, the average ICOHP is about −0.170 eV in Cs₂CO₃ and −0.177 eV in CsHCO₃. A more negative cumulative value over a larger contact network does not mean each individual bond is stronger; contact count, unit-cell choice and distance cutoff all feed into that sum.

The hydration comparison needs a different kind of bookkeeping. CO₂ adsorption referenced to each prepared hydration state measures affinity given that state. To predict populations, I would also have to pay for preparing each water count from a common reservoir, including the chemical potential of water. Strong adsorption in the one-water model does not mean one-water Cs⁺ is common.

Spectroscopy constrains the picture as well. The published assignment is a partially reduced, activated CO₂-derived intermediate; its notation does not require exactly one electron to sit on it. Its vibrational signal appears before sustained CO production. The Cs M-edge series was collected after returning to open circuit, because the faradaic current swamped detection under bias, so it probes an interface relaxing after polarization. Stabilization, population under bias and turnover remain separate questions.

A productive configuration needs a whole setting

Pb and Bi offer candidate mobile hydrogen donors. Cs⁺ offers a closer adsorbate contact while staying at a confined Ag interface. In both cases, a change in partners opens a chemically different possibility, and whether it pays off depends on the rest of the setting.

That closes the loop from water response, to Cu loss, to reactivity. In every part, I needed to know which configurations can be reached, whether their key species stay available, and how the cycle restores them. Keeping those three in view is what ties a molecular explanation back to the measured experiment.

Where this was published

This post follows thesis Chapters 5 and 6. The Pb impurity experiments appeared in Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2024); the Pb mechanism calculations in Catalysis Science & Technology 16, 4090–4102 (2026); and the p-block screen and Bi study in Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2026). I did the Pb reaction-path and p-block hydrogen-transfer calculations. The desolvated-cation study appeared in Nature Catalysis 9, 1009–1022 (2026); my contribution there was computational.
entry.summary: Part 3, Reactivity: Pb + Cs in CO2RR: hydride shuttles offer a route to amination, while partial Cs desolvation strengthens contact with activated CO2 in a separate Ag system

entry.title: When the cathode dissolves
entry.content:
The short version. Letting the cell sit for 18 minutes while it cooled dropped the later amine yield to 3.9 ± 0.2%. Holding a protective cathodic potential during cooling gave 30 ± 2%, and skipping the wait gave 51 ± 2%. Copper loss is part of the reason: about 84 ppm Cu ended up in solution without protection and 19 ppm with it, and about 13 ppm was still there after 30 minutes at −0.75 V versus RHE. My calculations trace how an amine walks a Cu atom out of a kink site. Pb was also present in these cells, so not every point of yield can be blamed on Cu.

In this post

  1. The cell changed while it cooled
  2. Negative potential helps, up to a point
  3. Start with a Cu atom at a kink
  4. Add partners, loosen the metal
  5. The vacancy stays on the receipt
  6. A stable product still needs an accessible path
  7. From losing metal to moving hydrogen
3.9 ± 0.2%amine yield after unprotected cooling
84 ppm → 19 ppmCu after cooling, without and with protection, approximately
13 ppmCu at −0.75 V versus RHE, approximately

The cell changed while it cooled

The experiment was supposed to start once the cell had cooled. The chemistry did not wait. After an 18-minute cooling period, the amine yield from the following electrolysis was only 3.9 ± 0.2%. Holding a protective cathodic potential during the same 18 minutes brought it up to 30 ± 2%. Skipping the cooling step altogether gave 51 ± 2%.

That is a big effect for a step that would normally disappear into one line of the experimental section. I wanted to know what the reaction mixture was doing to the electrode while everyone waited for the temperature to settle.

The cell for this reductive amination used a Cu cathode and a Pb anode separated by a Nafion N-324 membrane. The catholyte contained 2.4 M acetone and 2.9 M methylamine added to 0.5 M KH₂PO₄. The phosphate solution started at pH 8.3, but the final mixture measured pH 12.9 at 10 °C. The electrode sees the final mixture; the label on the buffer bottle does not get the last word.

After cooling, the solution held about 84 ppm Cu without protection and 19 ppm with it. That is direct evidence that metal was leaving the electrode during preparation. Cathodic protection helped, but it did not bring the loss to zero.

This follows on from Part 1. There, methylamine changed the water around Cu. Here the same nitrogen changes who Cu itself is bonded to, and the result is no longer just an electrical response: part of the electrode ends up in solution.

Negative potential helps, up to a point

A cathode is the reducing electrode, so dissolution sounds backwards at first. Making a dissolved Cu cation costs energy, and that cost grows as the potential becomes more negative. But that is only one side of the balance. Ligands can stabilize the dissolved metal enough to pay back a good part of the cost.

Potential-controlled experiments sharpened the question. After 30 minutes in the acetone–methylamine mixture, dissolved Cu fell as the applied potential moved from +0.25 toward −1.25 V versus RHE. Even so, about 13 ppm Cu remained at −0.75 V. The smallest loss came at −1.25 V.

So cathodic protection works here only conditionally. A negative potential works against forming the cationic products, while the chemical environment pushes the other way. To explain stability, I have to specify both the potential and the ligands around Cu.

The yield has another passenger

The cooling experiments also had a Pb anode and a membrane that had already been exposed to Pb. Later work showed that trace Pb can strongly promote this amination, which matters for reading the yield changes at the top of this post.

The dissolved-Cu measurements stand on their own as evidence of Cu loss. The yield, though, can depend on both the changing Cu surface and the amount of a mobile promoter in the cell. Pinning every percentage point on Cu dissolution would need Pb controlled at the same time. So I treat the cooling result as motivation, and as evidence that the cell remembers its history, rather than as a gauge of how much Cu dissolved.

It is also a reminder that the cell boundary matters. Anode, membrane, solution and cathode can trade chemically important material. Labelling each electrode does not keep their chemistry in separate rooms.

Start with a Cu atom at a kink

For the calculations, I compared a stepped and kinked Cu(843) surface with a flat Cu(111) terrace. A kink atom has six metallic neighbors; a terrace atom has nine. That gives a ligand a very different starting point for pulling an atom out.

I used ammonia first as a compact model ligand, then methylamine and ethylamine to see what alkyl groups change. Ammonia keeps the geometry simple; it does not mean the real reactant behaves identically in sterics or electronics.

The amine binds about 0.5 eV more strongly at the kink than on the terrace, with the exact difference depending on potential. Its nitrogen lone pair makes a specific bond to Cu, and more negative polarization weakens that donor bond over the modeled range. From the first step, the surface and the ligand are both responding to the same electrode potential.

Without an amine, moving a kink atom out onto the neighboring terrace as an adatom costs about 1 eV over the potentials studied. With one ammonia attached, it costs about 0.1–0.3 eV. The ligand props the atom up as it loses metallic neighbors.

That is the first useful piece of the mechanism. A ligand can lower the cost of making the surface precursor that later dissolves. Complexation in solution and extraction from the solid are two ends of one connected pathway.

The move also opens up new geometries. An adatom is more exposed than the kink atom it came from, leaving room for more nitrogen donors. And pulling an atom from the step edge exposes another kink-like site, so the motif can repeat rather than using up one special atom.

Add partners, loosen the metal

A second and third ammonia stabilize the extracted Cu atom further. A four-ligand structure can also form on the surface, although the remaining surface contacts constrain its shape. Once it detaches, the complex has room to adopt a solution-like geometry.

Bond analysis gives a useful electronic view. As Cu picks up nitrogen partners, its summed bonding to the surface goes down. For the four-ligand complex derived from the kink, the Cu–Cu −ICOHP contribution falls by about a factor of two relative to the low-ligand reference.

Cu–N bonds grow as the metallic bonds weaken. ICOHP describes that redistribution of bonding well, but it is not a bond-dissociation energy and not a computed detachment barrier.

I considered several dissolved coordination numbers and oxidation states. Among them, the linear two-ligand Cu(II) complex was the most stable, with three-ligand Cu(I) and four-ligand Cu(II) species competitive over parts of the potential range. These are candidate thermodynamic endpoints, not a measurement of which species dominates in the real solution.

The thresholds come out at about −1.1 V for the two-ammonia Cu(II) product, −0.9 V for the three-ammonia Cu(I) product and −0.8 V for the four-ammonia Cu(II) product, relative to the compared surface state at the modeled pH. On the positive side of each threshold, dissolution becomes favorable.

Those values explain why a negative potential can reduce dissolution without stopping it across the whole experimental window. They depend on the ligand chemical potential, product activity, pH and surface references used, and changing any of these shifts the balance.

Deep dive: the 0.51 and 0.21 eV comparison

For an illustrative four-ligand sequence at −0.7 V, the most uphill surface intermediate sits about 0.51 eV above the reference used in that profile. Letting the fourth ligand come in during detachment lowers that to about 0.21 eV. The order of coordination and detachment matters. Neither number is a computed transition-state barrier, so the comparison does not give a rate ratio.

The vacancy stays on the receipt

The terrace teaches a bookkeeping lesson. Taking an atom out of a perfect Cu(111) surface leaves a vacancy. If that vacancy stays in the model, the extraction sequence is strongly uphill, by roughly 1.5 eV for the relevant surface state.

If instead the vacancy is filled from a bulk Cu reservoir, the cost drops a lot. The two calculations describe different atom balances: the bulk reservoir has supplied something valuable, and the model has to say so.

A vacancy-compensated terrace calculation isolates the cost of the missing atom. It does not show that an atom can actually move into that vacancy on the experimental time scale.

The compensated terrace pathway resembles the kink sequence, but the flatter surroundings leave less room for several amine ligands, so the four-ligand surface precursor is less comfortable there. Its dissolved endpoint can still come close to the kink-derived threshold once the removed atom is referenced to bulk Cu.

On a real electrode, steps, edges and defects can supply atoms, and moving atoms between those sites has its own kinetics. The kink pathway is the clearest local picture of extraction; the compensated terrace is a useful thermodynamic limit. Keeping both makes the role of surface shape easier to see.

A stable product still needs an accessible path

Comparing ligands keeps the story from getting too tidy. Methylamine and ethylamine stabilize the dissolved complexes more strongly than ammonia, as their donor strength would suggest. Yet the first ligand-capped adatom costs more to make with the bulkier amines.

Experiments at −0.25 V found less dissolved Cu with the substituted amines than with ammonia. That fits a picture in which reaching the surface precursor is harder, even though the final dissolved complex is more stable.

This is why I keep endpoint stability and accessibility apart. A molecule can be a great partner for dissolved Cu and still struggle to get into the right geometry on a crowded metal surface. Steric and interfacial constraints bite before the system ever gets to enjoy the favorable endpoint.

The intermediate profiles support this qualitatively. They do not include every transition state needed to predict dissolution rates or long-term metal loss. That gap is a well-defined next problem: how fast can the ligands and the Cu atom move through this route under matched operating conditions?

From losing metal to moving hydrogen

What comes out of this is a chemically specific route for Cu loss under cathodic conditions. Amines bind low-coordinated Cu, make its displacement cheaper, and help swap metallic neighbors for ligands. The electrode potential works against some of that chemistry, but cannot be read independently of it.

The step from Part 1 is small at the molecular level and large in the lab. First methylamine rearranged the water around Cu. Now it rearranges who binds Cu. The interface can change its composition during preparation as well as during electrolysis.

A mobile metal species is not always a sign of a failing electrode, though. In Part 3, trace Pb offers a possible way of carrying hydrogen between Ag and an imine. Whether that helps depends on whether the species reacts productively and comes back. The question shifts from keeping every atom in place to knowing where it goes and whether it returns.

Where this was published

Origin of copper dissolution under electrocatalytic reduction conditions involving amines, Chemical Science 15, 14485–14496 (2024). This post follows thesis Chapter 4. I did the calculations and wrote the first draft of the manuscript; the measurements are reported in the same paper. The Pb caveat connects to the 2024 impurity study discussed in Part 3.
entry.summary: Part 2, Dissolution: amines help Cu exchange metallic neighbors for nitrogen ligands, so negative polarization reduces metal loss without always eliminating it

entry.title: Capacitance before reduction
entry.content:
The short version. Acetone raises the double-layer capacitance of Cu, and methylamine lowers it, even though both molecules are more polarizable than water. To see why, I modeled the water around them. With frozen water geometries, one explicit layer gives about 7.4 µF cm⁻² and a three-layer snapshot average gives about 4.2 µF cm⁻², against about 13.35 µF cm⁻² for continuum solvent alone. Placed in those layers, acetone pushes the response up and methylamine pushes it down, mostly through what they do to their water neighbors. All of this happens before the potential is anywhere near where the organic reduction runs.

In this post

  1. Two solutes, opposite signs
  2. First, give Cu some water
  3. Acetone changes the neighborhood
  4. Methylamine rearranges it
  5. A response is not a head count
  6. Before reduction, the interface has changed
7.4 µF cm⁻²one-layer water reference, approximately
4.2 µF cm⁻²three-layer frozen-snapshot average, approximately
−0.32 Vmeasured minimum versus RHE, approximately

Two solutes, opposite signs

The first puzzle was a sign. Add acetone to the electrolyte around Cu and the measured capacitance goes up. Add methylamine and it goes down. If either solute simply replaced some water with a more polarizable molecule, both should push the same way. The experiment was telling me early on that the neighbors mattered more than the molecule.

This is the quiet start of the series. Acetone and methylamine are the two reactants of a reductive amination: they condense to an imine, which is then reduced to an amine. Before asking how that reduction works, I wanted to know what each reactant does to the place where it will happen.

The impedance measurements used polished Cu in 0.01 M NaClO₄, brought to pH 12 with KOH, over a window from −0.227 to −0.527 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The capacitance minimum sat near −0.32 V. That is a convenient place to start: close to zero charge, and before a large faradaic current takes over the signal.

Capacitance measures how much extra charge an interface takes on when the potential changes. At the molecular scale, that depends on much more than how soft one electron cloud is. Where molecules sit, which way the water points, how tightly things pack, and how far the charge is screened all enter. My task was to find chemically reasonable structures that explain both signs.

First, give Cu some water

I started with water on Cu(111), with a dielectric continuum beyond it standing in for the rest of the solution. Explicit water lets me tell apart molecules pointing a hydrogen toward the metal (H-down) from those pointing their oxygen toward it (O-down). These are orientation classes, not permanent job titles; molecules switch between them.

The sampled one-layer structures give 7.3–7.5 µF cm⁻², averaging about 7.4. The three-layer frozen-snapshot average is about 4.2. Continuum solvent alone gives about 13.35. So adding explicit water lowers the calculated capacitance.

That looks backwards if more water should mean more bulk-like screening. The detail that resolves it is what the calculation lets move. Molecular dynamics lets the water explore local arrangements. I then compute the charging response with the nuclei frozen in each sampled geometry. The electrons respond, but the molecules cannot turn to follow the field. A high-dielectric continuum includes exactly the kind of response those frozen nuclei cannot give.

Thickness matters, and the model notices

In the layer series, one to four explicit layers give about 7.4, 5.2, 4.1 and 3.5 µF cm⁻², read from the supporting plot. The three-layer value in that series and the snapshot average above come from different comparisons, so I keep them labelled separately rather than treating them as one number.

The drop from three to four layers is a useful warning. It shows sensitivity to how the explicit region is built, not convergence to a single bulk value. More explicit layers make a thicker frozen region, and that region screens differently from the continuum it replaces.

The familiar capacitors-in-series picture helps here. The inverse capacitance adds up a thickness-over-screening term from each region, so a thin region that screens poorly can dominate. Real molecular layers have no obligation to come with sharp edges or a single dielectric constant, so I use the picture to explain the direction of the trend, not to assign each water layer a permittivity.

Acetone changes the neighborhood

With the water reference in hand, I replaced one layer of the three-layer model with acetone, placed next to Cu, in the middle, or near the outer edge. That changes position while keeping everything else about the model the same.

Every placement raises the capacitance relative to pure water. Acetone next to Cu gives the largest increase, the middle placement the next largest. That makes sense: a change close to the stored electrode charge has the most direct effect on screening.

Acetone brings a polar carbonyl and two methyl groups. Its isolated-molecule polarizability is near 7.9 Å³, against roughly 1 Å³ for water. But the carbonyl contact and the space taken by the methyl groups also change the water next to it. Molecular polarizabilities do not add up like items on a grocery receipt.

One-layer mixtures give an independent check. Acetone can approach with its carbonyl roughly vertical or lie flatter on Cu, leaving different room for water. Every arrangement tested still gives higher capacitance and polarizability than its water-only reference. Agreement in sign across different constructions is more convincing than the exact size from any one of them.

The sizes are still instructive. A representative three-layer arrangement raises capacitance by about 21% but polarizability by about 200%. A representative one-layer arrangement gives about 11% and 16%. The two quantities move together without a fixed ratio, because they describe different responses under different boundary conditions.

I also checked what the trajectories were actually doing. Acetone stayed in its assigned region throughout the sampled motion. The bottom, middle and top models therefore describe different local arrangements; they say what each arrangement would do if present, not how often it occurs in the experiment.

Methylamine rearranges it

Methylamine is the more revealing case, because it defeats the isolated-molecule argument outright. It is more polarizable than water, yet the measured capacitance falls as its concentration rises near the minimum.

Its nitrogen has options. The lone pair can bind Cu or accept a hydrogen bond, the N–H groups can donate hydrogen bonds, and a local proton transfer can make a methylammonium–hydroxide pair. Those options let methylamine reshape the water network in ways the acetone arrangements do not.

In the three-layer models, every methylamine configuration tested lowers both capacitance and polarizability relative to water, with the largest drops close to Cu. One-layer calculations keep the same direction, whether the molecule is bound to Cu through nitrogen or held near the surface by its water.

The water orientation gives a structural clue. Around acetone, H-down and O-down populations stay roughly balanced. Methylamine produces a lasting H-down bias, especially in the unbound middle and bottom arrangements. The water is part of the solute effect.

Some methylamine configurations also form local ion pairs. That is chemically relevant, but I would not make one ion pair the sole cause of the whole response. Proton transfer, orientation, packing and Cu–water contacts all change together, and a Cu-bound methylamine uses its lone pair differently from an unbound one. The shared decrease across all these cases is more robust than any single microscopic story.

It helps to separate organizing from responding. The nuclei rearrange first and set up the local electronic environment. The frozen-geometry calculation then measures how the electrons in that environment respond. It does not measure slow water rotation under an applied field. The molecules arrange the room before I test how its electrons react.

A response is not a head count

A capacitance measurement can tell me that the interface changed without telling me which structure it became. Several arrangements can give the same sign. To get their populations I would need thorough sampling, consistent chemical potentials, and free energies for moving molecules between environments.

The trajectory diagnostics keep this honest. Bounded energy fluctuations support local sampling, and layer-averaged heights show that the assigned regions stay recognizable. Neither shows that every relevant solvent-exchange barrier has been crossed. A middle layer whose height overlaps its neighbors is not, by itself, evidence that molecules swap layers freely.

Deep dive: what the experimental capacitance includes

The impedance data were fitted with a resistance and a constant phase element rather than an ideal capacitor. Effective capacitance came from the fitted resistance and the characteristic frequency of the semicircle, normalized by geometric area. That number depends on the equivalent circuit and on real-electrode heterogeneity. I compare it with the frozen-configuration calculations through trends first, without assuming the absolute values are the same observable.

The same care applies to formation energies. Optimizing a structure taken from a final snapshot characterizes an endpoint; it does not turn it into a trajectory-averaged free energy. A more negative formation energy after adding water also partly reflects having more molecules. Neither gives the equilibrium population of water layers.

The direction of each solute effect survives every model choice I tested. The exact microscopic populations and the full frequency-dependent response are still open. That is enough to support a collective, interface-level explanation, and it leaves a clear next task for sampling and experiment.

Before reduction, the interface has changed

What I take from this is that reactants start doing chemistry well before their reduction step. Acetone and methylamine rearrange the contacts around Cu, and that changes the electrical response. The electrolyte is already shaping the surface on which the later reaction will run.

It would be tempting to carry the capacitance trend straight into a prediction of amine yield, and the work does not support that jump. Organic reduction runs at more cathodic potentials in different mixtures. A changed charging response does not imply a changed imine-hydrogenation barrier, and higher capacitance is not automatically better catalysis.

Methylamine does leave a useful lead. Its nitrogen talks to water and to Cu. In Part 2, I follow that same coordination chemistry into a less comfortable question: what happens when the amine helps a Cu atom leave?

Where this was published

Probing the Electric Double-Layer Capacitance to Understand the Reaction Environment in Conditions of Electrochemical Amination of Acetone, ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces 17, 4087–4097 (2025). This post follows thesis Chapter 3. I did the calculations and computational analysis; the measurements are reported in the same paper.
entry.summary: Part 1, Capacitance: acetone and methylamine change Cu double-layer capacitance in opposite directions, and the surrounding water explains why molecular polarizability is not enough

entry.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

link.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

entry.content:
For my internship I left my UCLA computational chemistry desk for a while and joined SES AI, a battery company, as an Applied Scientist intern. The problem was that today's AI is very good with pictures and text, while chemistry and batteries live in 3D geometry, in physical time, and in scales that connect, where a tiny change in one molecule shows up much later as a battery that lasts longer (or doesn't). So the work ended up as a grid rather than a straight line: three scales stacked on top of each other, each known through several kinds of data, with the same small method run at every level.

In this post

  1. The picture in one diagram
  2. The scale axis: molecule, electrolyte, cell
  3. The modality axis: many ways to know each layer
  4. The same loop at every layer
  5. How representations flow upward
  6. The three parts
  7. What this got us

The picture in one diagram

The official title I gave the work was “multiscale multimodal intelligence across molecules, electrolytes, and cells,” which is a mouthful, so here it is as one picture instead.

Read it in three directions. Up the rows is the scale axis: what the thing is. Across the columns is the modality axis: how we get to know it. And the loop on the right of every row is the method, the same four steps each time. The short sections below take one direction at a time.

The scale axis: molecule, electrolyte, cell

Each row is a layer, and each layer is made of the one below it: molecules make up electrolytes, and electrolytes go into cells.

Think of a battery like a city. The molecules are the people. The electrolyte is the crowd, the liquid the ions swim through, made of salt, solvents and additives. The cell is the whole city, with its traffic jams, heat waves and aging infrastructure. You can’t understand a city from one person’s ID card, and you can’t understand a crowd without watching it move, so the work split into three parts, one per layer, each building on the last.

The modality axis: many ways to know each layer

At every layer, no single kind of data tells the whole story, and the layers don’t even share the same kinds. Here is what each row of the diagram actually holds.

Molecule

  • Images and text: molecule drawings in real papers (hand-drawn ones too) and what the paper says about them
  • 1D/2D/3D structure: SMILES and fingerprints, atom graphs, 3D conformers
  • DFT and MD properties: energies, HOMO/LUMO, how readily it gets reduced; solvation, density, diffusion, transport

Electrolyte

  • Recipes: components, amounts and conditions like temperature
  • DFT clusters: the ion with one partner, or a solvent and an anion competing for it
  • MD trajectories: about 40,000 of them, 5,000 frames each, roughly 200 million frames
  • Conductivity data, including the public CALiSol dataset

Cell

  • Multiscale simulations: DFT, MD, interface reactions, kMC, P2D/SPMe and 3D temperature and stress fields
  • Experiments: a 252-formulation, additive-centered DOE
  • Design and test conditions: protocol, temperature, C-rate

None of this is text in the way a chatbot would like. That was the question I kept asking all internship: can AI understand not just pictures and text, but 3D geometry, physical time, and how the scales connect?

The same loop at every layer

Only when I laid the three parts side by side did I notice that every layer runs the same loop: gather the data, learn a representation, align the different views of the same thing, then hand it to a co-scientist that helps decide what to do next. Prediction sits on top of the aligned space at every layer.

  Data Representation Alignment Co-scientist / decision
Molecule paper figures read by VLMs, checked by VERDICT 1D/2D/3D vectors 2D ↔ 3D partners (InfoNCE), keyed by InChIKey multimodal database in MU and a Chrome extension
Electrolyte polarizable force field, ~40,000 MD movies recipe, snapshot and trajectory heads three-way contrastive, one 128-d latent electrolyte co-scientist
Cell 252-formulation DOE plus a simulation ladder stacked molecule, electrolyte and cell reps cross-scale links, conditions as the glue aging world model, cell co-scientist, decision API

One lesson also kept showing up at every layer: a pretty number on the training objective is not the same as the scientific goal. A preference model can score beautifully and still get molecules wrong. A force field can nail tiny clusters and still ruin the liquid. An alignment can match molecules perfectly and still say almost nothing about real batteries. So most of my summer went into the checks: agreement between independent readers, liquid simulations inside the fitting loop, calibration against real measurements.

How representations flow upward

The layers aren’t three separate projects, because what one layer learns becomes input to the next. Nothing from the lower rows gets thrown away.

Molecule vectors become ingredients

Part 1 turns every recognized molecule into vectors. In the electrolyte layer those vectors become ingredients on the recipe side: a formulation network takes one vector per molecule, plus mixing ratios, salt concentration and temperature, and predicts how the mixture behaves.

The electrolyte latent and molecules build the cell

Part 2 turns every electrolyte into 128 numbers in a shared latent space, learned from recipes, snapshots and trajectories. In Part 3 a cell is represented by stacking those pieces: the molecule representations for each component, the electrolyte latent for the mixture, and the cell’s own design and operating conditions on top. The cell co-scientist reads the same stack, with 396 molecular, 274 electrolyte and 105 cell features per record in its early version.

The three parts

Each part walks through one row of the diagram in detail, in the order the stuff itself is built.

Part 1: molecules

Atom is atom, bond is bond. Reading molecules off real paper figures (59.8% exact on 331 journal figures), VERDICT’s four readers that may abstain, a rotation-aware recognizer, and 1D/2D/3D vectors in a multimodal database.

Part 2: electrolytes

Teaching a puddle to dance. A polarizable force field for 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, PFF RSI learning from more than 50 failed versions out of 80, three heads over about 40,000 MD movies, and an electrolyte co-scientist.

Part 3: cells

From molecules to batteries. A six-rung simulation ladder around a 252-formulation DOE, scales held together by test conditions, an aging world model that learns the whole evolution step by step, and a cell co-scientist.

What this got us

I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin; the method should transfer to similar multiscale systems, the ones built as molecules, then mixtures, then devices, where the important structure lives in drawings, geometry and simulations rather than text, and where experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. It’s still a living method, and I keep adding pieces as the field moves. Grab a snack: Part 1 starts at the bottom row, with a molecule and a computer trying to figure out who it is.
entry.summary: Overview of a three-part series on my Applied Scientist internship at SES AI: molecules make up electrolytes, electrolytes go into batteries, and each part builds on the representations of the one before

entry.title: From molecules to batteries
entry.content:
The electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real cells here, and the question becomes the one a battery company actually cares about: if I change the recipe, what changes in the battery? Starting from 252 additive-centered formulations, I stacked the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 into a cell representation, built a ladder of multiscale simulations around the real recipes, aligned the scales, trained an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and wrapped it all in a cell co-scientist. The clearest finding was that test conditions are the glue between scales: removing them collapsed a key cross-scale link score from 0.327 to 0.066.

In this post

  1. Δrecipe → Δperformance
  2. A cell is a stack of representations
  3. Simulations around the real recipes, lined up
  4. An aging world model
  5. Checking against real cells
  6. A cell co-scientist
  7. What this got us
252additive-centered DOE formulations
3,331electrothermal simulations linked to DOE records
0.327 → 0.066MD-to-electrode link score without conditions
41world-model architectures compared
24targets supported by sim-to-real calibration

Δrecipe → Δperformance

My starting point was a real, specific problem: a design of experiments (DOE) of 252 cell formulations built around additives, and a lot of questions about it.

Change the recipe, watch the battery

Within each comparison the electrodes were held fixed and the additives changed, so any change in performance can be pinned on the recipe. The question is simple to say: change the recipe, and what changes in capacity retention, cycle life, resistance and rate? In practice that meant looking at cycling, storage, charging and rate tests.

Slow bakes, plenty of compute

It’s a bit like baking. Swap one ingredient and the cake might rise higher, or collapse, or taste fine today and go stale next month. The annoying part is that each real bake for a battery is slow and expensive, and there was no budget for repeated new rounds of experiments. Compute, on the other hand, was available. So the plan was to use compute to fill in around the real data, while real measurements stay the reference. Simulations get to advise; they don’t get to overrule.

A cell is a stack of representations

The idea that unlocked this part is that nothing from Parts 1 and 2 had to be thrown away. Both were, at heart, representation learning.

Reuse, don’t restart

Part 1 turned every molecule into vectors from its 1D, 2D and 3D views. Part 2 turned every electrolyte into 128 numbers in a shared latent space, learned from recipes, snapshots and trajectories. A battery cell can be represented by stacking those learned pieces: the molecule representations for each component, the electrolyte latent for the mixture, and the cell’s own design and operating conditions on top.

Molecules make up electrolytes and electrolytes go into cells, and here the representations follow the same path.

Simulations around the real recipes, lined up

A stack of representations needs something to learn from, and 252 formulations is not a lot, so I spent about a month building a high-throughput ladder of high-fidelity simulations around the DOE itself: around its real recipes and its real test protocols, not around made-up chemistry. No single simulation covers everything from electrons to a whole cell heating up, so each rung hands something to the next.

Six rungs

Here are the six rungs, from the smallest scale to the largest.

1. DFT

Electrons and local chemistry: whether an additive can be reduced, who coordinates around the ion, and how much energy it takes for a molecule to decompose. That local chemistry is the starting point for the liquid.

2. MD

How molecules organize and move in the liquid: solvation, aggregation, diffusion and conductivity. This is the PFF from Part 2, and it supplies what arrives at the electrode.

3. Interface reactions

How molecules may change near the electrode, the battery’s busiest border crossing, where bonds break and form. I explored these with a learned force model, and the events it finds become the moves for the next rung.

4. kMC

Kinetic Monte Carlo thinks in states, events and rates, like a board game where each move happens with some probability per unit time, to ask what happens next over long times. In my setup, kMC sits inside the cell model, the next rung.

5. P2D / SPMe

The whole cell’s transport and reactions: voltage, capacity and aging. P2D resolves what happens through the electrode’s thickness and inside its particles; SPMe is its simpler, cheaper cousin for when you need many runs fast. Both treat the cell as one stack.

6. 3D fields

Temperature and stress varying across the cell. I ran 3,331 electrothermal simulations linked to DOE records, using the recorded protocols, with stated assumptions about geometry and thermal inputs.

Deep dive: what the kMC rung did and didn't show

When I compressed MD transport into 12 states, the model’s held-out transition NLL was 1.612 versus 2.273 for an independent-state baseline (lower is better). Full SEI growth was not validated, so I’m not claiming it.

Every calculation keeps its recipe, conditions, source and a fidelity label: measured, calculated or predicted. Mixing those up is how you end up trusting a simulation more than the experiment it was supposed to explain.

Lining up the scales

With simulations at every scale, the next step was to connect them, the same way Part 2 connected recipes, frames and motion. Each input got its own encoder, mapped into a shared 128-d space. Then I learned links between neighboring scales: DFT ↔ molecules, molecules ↔ formulations, formulations + conditions ↔ MD, MD + conditions ↔ cells, cells + conditions ↔ DOE, plus links for the interface. The loss was a multi-positive InfoNCE, a fancy way of saying “pull together everything that belongs to the same experiment, push apart everything that doesn’t,” along with predicting the next scale’s vector from the current one.

To keep myself honest I trained four versions, three seeds each: the full model, no conditions, shuffled pairs, and no extra linking loss. Two findings stood out.

Conditions are the glue. Temperature, C-rate and protocol are what connect the scales: removing them collapsed the MD-to-electrode link score from 0.327 to 0.066. Without knowing how a battery was tested, the scales stop recognizing each other. Correct pairs also scored much better than shuffled ones, so the links are real.

The second finding is that molecules don’t get you to a battery just via alignment. Matching a molecule’s identity across views could be strong while the links to the real DOE stayed weaker.

Property heads

On top of the shared space sit regression and classification heads for property prediction. With chemistry inputs only, the normalized error (MAE across DOE targets) fell from 0.3341 to 0.2849 using modality dropout, which means randomly hiding inputs during training so the model learns to cope when some are missing. It cost a little when every input was available (0.2442 → 0.2542), a trade I’ll happily take. And the uncertainty was overconfident: nominal 90% intervals covered only about 68–78%, so the stated uncertainty needs widening before anyone relies on it.

An aging world model

The heads still predict a target as one number, and that’s the habit this section breaks: the goal shifted from predicting lifetime to learning the whole evolution process, how the cell’s state evolves under its design and its conditions.

From one number to the whole story

The usual black box takes the recipe in and gives one number out (“lifetime: N cycles”). It gives you nothing to check along the way, and when it’s wrong, it can’t tell you why.

Simulations as the practice data

To learn a process you need to watch it happen many times, and real experiments are few and slow. Simulations, on the other hand, give dense, state-by-state trajectories under many designs and conditions. So I ran a large number of P2D and 3D aging simulations: expensive, long DFN (full P2D) runs for some cases and cheaper, short SPMe runs for many more, screening early and recording why each run stopped. The 3D layer added 100,000 electrothermal entries and 200,000 chemical-mechanical results. The DOE stays the real-cell reference throughout.

How it works

Aging world model

Given the cell’s design, its current state (voltage, capacity, temperature, aging variables, state of health) and the condition (how it’s being used: protocol, temperature, C-rate), it predicts the next state. Then it rolls out: each prediction becomes the next input, step by step, into a full aging curve, and the lifetime is read off where the curve hits an endpoint, for example 80% of initial capacity. The same machinery covers calendar aging (sitting on a shelf) and cycle aging (being used).

It’s like predicting tomorrow’s weather, then using that forecast to predict the day after.

I compared 41 architectures on an early dataset of 6,258 simulated sequences × 140 steps, and the learned world model beat a direct MLP baseline on simulated sequences. My historical summary recorded roughly 24–27% lower error. I haven’t yet traced every one of those numbers back to its fold and target, and to be very clear, it is a lower prediction error on simulations, not an increase in anyone’s real cycle life.

Four checks

Next-step accuracy

Does one step forward land in the right place?

Long-run drift

Harsh, because each output becomes the next input and small errors snowball.

Direction of change

Does the curve move the right way when you swap an additive or a condition?

Agreement with experiments

Does it match real cells, not just the simulator?

The honest gap is that a model that learns the simulator very well can also inherit the simulator’s mistakes. How well it learns the simulations and how well it matches real cells are separate questions.

Knowledge emergence, carefully

Here’s the part that got me most excited, and I want to be careful with it. Because the model learns the process instead of memorizing endpoints, I started to see it pick up physically sensible chemistry and battery behavior that nobody spelled out for it, which is what I’d call knowledge emergence.

That’s my observation and interpretation, not a measured result. What I can point to is how it gets checked: rollouts are inspected for unphysical behavior in capacity, temperature and concentration at different horizons, held-out operating conditions test whether the model responds in the right direction, and the direction-of-change check is one of the four tests above. I’m not claiming it discovered anything specific like SEI growth or lithium plating. Confirming emergence rigorously is ongoing work, and probably my favorite open question from the summer.

Checking against real cells

Simulations are the practice field, not the match, so the last scientific step was to hold the models up against the DOE.

The VC plot twist

My favorite plot twist came from one additive, VC. In matched DOE comparisons it hurt cycle life in one cell design and helped in another. Same ingredient, opposite story. A physics model built on a fixed VC-SEI hypothesis reproduced some of the sign changes, but not the full direction and size of the effect. That sounds like a failure, but it’s the most useful kind of result: it turns the hypothesis into a candidate mechanism with a concrete next test.

Calibration, not self-grading

A rule I try hard to follow: don’t tune a model on the DOE and then hold up the same DOE as validation. That’s grading your own homework with the answer key taped to the back.

The bridge between simulation and reality is calibration against real experiments, and the sim-to-real calibration supported 24 targets. Everything else stays labeled for what it is: simulated until a real cell says otherwise.

A cell co-scientist

The last piece was the same move as at the end of Part 2, one scale up: hand everything to a co-scientist that can reason over it. This time the inputs come from every level.

Inputs from every level

In the early version, each record carried numbers from all three parts, 775 in all.

396 molecular

Molecular features from Part 1.

274 electrolyte

Electrolyte features from Part 2.

105 cell

Cell features from this part.

Each group goes through its own small projector into 4 “soft tokens,” and the 12 soft prefix tokens sit in front of the text, with missing inputs masked. Tokenization is chemistry-aware: common molecule names are kept as single tokens, with markers for chemistry and scale, so names get read as chemistry rather than letter soup.

Deep dive: text evidence, explanation examples and the training split

Next to the numbers goes text evidence: the recipe, the conditions, measured and simulated results, and where each came from. I also built explanation examples from evidence packages: a teacher model writes the explanation, and a critic plus fixed rules check it. A first pilot had 300 examples covering complete, missing, novel and conflicting evidence. On top of that come the data, the simulation logs and the tool-usage records. Held-out experimental answers stayed out of training, forward prediction can’t see the target value, and the split is by recipe. The fine-tuning itself is LoRA (QLoRA) on the LLM, trained together with the scientific projectors.

The harness and the split between two models

Cell co-scientist

The harness is DeepSeek Harness, connected to battery tools: cell prediction, recipe suggestions, similar experiments, cross-scale explanations, multiscale evidence, and formulation comparison, plus a call to the trained specialist that attaches the record’s evidence chain. A workspace keeps the conversation, the explanations and the tool history.

The work is split between two models: a larger LLM handles planning and tool calls, and the fine-tuned compact open-weight LLM acts as the scientific specialist. Its training data didn’t include tool-call trajectories, and I learned that good scientific answers don’t automatically give you reliable tool use.

What it can do

It connects recipes, conditions, simulated states and measurements; explains an answer with sources; compares candidate formulations; suggests recipes; finds similar experiments; and says what evidence is missing and what the next useful calculation would be. The interface shows the explanation, the tool calls, the returned results and the record IDs, and it marks every piece of evidence as measured, computed, predicted, missing or rejected. If you’ve read this far, you know why that matters to me.

To be honest about where it stands: in the demo, prediction and inverse design still used DOE retrieval and ranking of measured recipes, and connecting the world model is further work. A first explanation-training pilot didn’t improve the combined score, so it stayed experimental. And the reasoning text it writes is an output to inspect, not proof of what happened inside the model.

A decision API for the small judgments

Watching the agent work gave me one more idea, which is design thinking rather than a measured result. A lot of what an agent does all day is small and repetitive: is this record relevant, which of these four candidates fits, how complete is this evidence on a five-level scale. Those steps need judgment or a score, not long reasoning, and they’re exactly where a general LLM can wander off and return something malformed.

Jev decision API

I’d route those steps through a decision API to Jev, TypeSafe AI’s decision model, released on 15 September 2026 as a “System One” decision model. Jev answers typed questions about a text or JSON state and only returns structured outputs: a Choice (pick from up to 255 options, with probabilities), a Score (a position on a rubric of 2 to 10 levels that you describe), or a yes/no probability.

An independent evaluation reports 95–99% accuracy on several classification benchmarks and well-calibrated choice probabilities. Its “can’t hallucinate” guarantee is about format: the output always matches the declared schema, so no invented options and no parse errors. It isn’t a guarantee of correctness, and it can still pick a valid but wrong answer, which is why those steps still get checked. The point of the split is that the small judgments never come back malformed and come with calibrated probabilities, and the reasoning LLM is freed to do what it’s good at, which should make the whole agent stronger.

I’d like to say this is now a finished method of my own: represent, align, predict, then a co-scientist with a decision API. Honestly, the field moves so fast that I spent the summer chasing the frontier and bolting new pieces on, and I expect to keep doing that. It’s a living method, and this is its current version.

What this got us

The summer followed the stuff itself. Molecules got recognized and represented (Part 1), mixed into electrolytes whose rulebook, movies and latent space I built (Part 2), and went into cells, where the representations stacked up, the scales got aligned, a world model learned how the whole thing ages, and a co-scientist learned to reason over all of it (Part 3). Looking back, the same pattern showed up at every scale: represent, align, predict, and hand it to a co-scientist.

I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin, and I think the pieces add up to a framework that should transfer to similar systems: complex material and chemical systems built as molecules, then mixtures or formulations, then devices, where the structure lives in non-text data like drawings, geometry, trajectories and simulations, the scales are linked by conditions, and experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. Through all of it, real experiments stayed the reference: simulations explore, models propose, measurements decide. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have a mechanism test to think about.
entry.summary: Part 3, cells: the electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real batteries, and the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 stack up into a representation of the cell. Multiscale simulations around a 252-formulation experiment, alignment between scales, an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and a cell co-scientist that closes the series

entry.title: Teaching a puddle to dance
entry.content:
In Part 1 molecules got recognized and turned into vectors; here they get mixed into electrolytes, and the question becomes how they move. I extended a polarizable force field to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, turned the failures of more than 50 of 80 versions into a self-improving fitting loop, and taught a model to read about 40,000 molecular-dynamics movies through three heads and one shared 128-number space. That space predicts conductivity with R² 0.976, and everything I learned along the way became training material for an electrolyte co-scientist.

In this post

  1. How do molecules move in a liquid?
  2. Writing a bigger rulebook
  3. The liquid gets a vote
  4. PFF RSI: turning failures into checks
  5. 40,000 movies and three heads
  6. The electrolyte co-scientist
  7. What this got us
627+molecules and 20+ anions in the force field
50+ of 80force-field versions failed in the liquid
~40,000MD trajectories, roughly 200 million frames
R² 0.976conductivity from the shared 128-d space
18 of 21held-out chemistry groups improved by trajectory features

How do molecules move in a liquid?

The question I worked on for this part was how molecules move in their micro-environment, and it starts with what an electrolyte actually is.

A crowded dance floor

An electrolyte is the liquid inside a battery that ions swim through. The recipe is simple: salt + solvents + additives, and those are exactly the molecules from Part 1, now with jobs. The behavior is not simple. Zoom in and it’s a crowded dance floor: lithium ions grab solvent molecules as partners, anions try to cut in, and how fast everyone gets across the floor decides how well the battery charges and discharges.

A rulebook and a movie

To watch that dance on a computer you need two things. A force field is the rulebook for how atoms push and pull on each other. Molecular dynamics (MD) is playing the movie with that rulebook: put lots of molecules in a box, apply the rules, and watch. If the rulebook is wrong, the movie is fiction. Very confident, beautifully rendered fiction.

Writing a bigger rulebook

My first job was to grow the rulebook so that the molecules people actually want to try have rules to follow. The force field is polarizable (PFF), meaning electron clouds can squish in response to their neighbors, which matters a lot around small, charged ions like lithium. The goal was coverage: extend it to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, for both lithium and sodium electrolytes.

Reference data from quantum chemistry

The reference data comes from quantum chemistry (DFT), and lots of it. Some clusters are binary: the ion with one partner. Some are ternary: a solvent and an anion competing for the same ion, like two people reaching for the last slice of pizza. Each pair or trio gets computed at many distances and orientations, so the rulebook sees close calls, near misses and awkward side-on approaches, not just the polite pose.

What actually got fit

What I fit was mainly the exp-6 cross terms, keeping the charges and the polarization background fixed. All the while I was debugging, learning electrolyte science on the fly, and studying the properties that came out. Three jobs at once, which is roughly how every internship works.

Deep dive: what exp-6 means

Exp-6 is the part of the rulebook that covers short-range repulsion (“personal space!”) and dispersion, the weak, sticky attraction between everything. The “exp” is an exponential wall that keeps atoms from overlapping; the “6” is a gentle pull that falls off with the sixth power of distance.

The liquid gets a vote

The hardest lesson of the summer was that a fit isn’t done when the cluster error is low; it’s done when the liquid behaves. Density, radial distribution functions (who stands next to whom), diffusion, conductivity and viscosity all have to come out sensible in MD. My ledger ended up indexing 80 distinct force-field versions, and more than 50 of them failed. Here are a few of my favorite ways to fail.

The penguin huddle

One fit looked great on the clusters. Errors low, curves lined up, very satisfying. Then I ran the liquid and it clumped: the ions huddled together like penguins in a blizzard. I traced it to one ether-oxygen interaction the fit had effectively broken. Restoring it cut the ion aggregation fraction from 0.811 to 0.282, and from 0.415 to 0.044 in a second system. Conductivity moved closer to experiment, though it was still too low. Progress, not victory.

The wall that rounded to zero

A tiny coefficient, 0.00170, got rounded to zero on its way into the simulation. The builder treated zero as “missing” and helpfully swapped a big repulsive wall for a small one, and MD failed. Now a check reads the final built parameters, not just the ones I meant to build.

The helium incident

Lone-pair virtual sites stored with the label “He” were passed to DFT as real helium atoms. That quietly affected 27 of 61 clusters. Nothing says summer internship like accidentally inventing noble-gas electrolyte chemistry. Now templates, masses and site types are checked before anything goes out.

The failure that was a success

A salt-free solvent control came out at a viscosity of about 2.1–2.4 mPa·s, which told me the solvent was fine and the problem lived in the salt model.

An electrolyte has many jobs, and a rulebook that only nails small clusters can still flunk all of them in the liquid. What I learned is that a low DFT fitting error doesn’t protect the liquid, and MD validation is part of parameter development, not a final demo.

PFF RSI: turning failures into checks

Fifty-odd failures is a lot of pain, but it’s also a lot of data, so I distilled them into a recursive self-improvement system, PFF RSI.

PFF RSI

At its core it’s a simple cycle: fit the force field, validate in MD, record the failures, refine the next fit. When a brand-new molecule shows up, the loop runs on its own: sample, fit, guard, check in MD, learn, repeat.

Four layers under the cycle

Underneath the cycle, I built four layers.

Memory

A saved failure: the system, the version, what changed, what I expected versus what I measured, and what it cost, stored so it can be searched later by conditions, bad parameters, symptoms and useful checks.

Context

Loading the relevant failures before a new fit.

Code harness

Turning a failure into an automatic check, a new procedure written as code, so the same mistake gets caught by a machine instead of by me at 11 pm.

Weights

The fitted parameters that the whole loop keeps refining.

A new molecule arrives

When a brand-new molecule shows up, the loop samples a small starting set of clusters and expands only the channels that failed, fits, and checks. Parameters that match a known failure pattern get intercepted and sent to MD for a look before anyone uses them, so the wall that rounded to zero and the helium incident can’t sneak through twice. The honest caveat is that a fixed-budget test proving this memory actually makes research faster is still on my to-do list. It feels faster. Feelings aren’t data.

40,000 movies and three heads {#40000-movies-and-three-heads}

Once the rulebook works you can make movies, lots of them, and then you hit a new problem: none of it is text. Each trajectory is 5,000 frames, one every 4 picoseconds, for 20 nanoseconds in total. I ended up with about 40,000 trajectories, roughly 200 million frames.

You can’t paste a trajectory into a chatbot and ask how it felt. It’s coordinates, boxes and time, and the interesting part (who solvates whom, how ions hop) is spread across thousands of frames. So I asked whether a model could learn what a liquid is by watching, and squeeze each one into something small enough to search, compare and predict with.

Three views of the same liquid

I looked at the same liquid through three views, each with its own encoder, or “head.”

1. Recipe

What’s in the bottle: the components, their amounts, and conditions like temperature, turned into 128 numbers.

2. Snapshot

One frozen frame of 3D atoms. It’s my favorite, so it gets its own subsection below.

3. Trajectory

Motion over time: the 5,000 frames are split into 50 chunks of 100, so the model sees how things move, not just a pose.

All three are compressed into one shared 128-d latent space and trained with three-way contrastive alignment: views of the same liquid are pulled together, views of different liquids pushed apart. A recipe should find its own movie, and a snapshot should find its own recipe. That one space then does three jobs: retrieval, alignment between views, and property prediction.

What the space can do

For retrieval, retrieval@10 (is the matching liquid in the top 10?) was 84.1% with the full representation versus 82.4% from the static snapshot alone, so a single frame already knows a lot. For conductivity, the model reached R² 0.976, close to a strong descriptor baseline, and adding trajectory features improved conductivity error in 18 of 21 held-out chemistry groups: motion helps, especially on chemistry the model hasn’t seen. Across the property heads, I got R² 0.906, 0.936 and 0.987 for conductivity, viscosity and solubility. The representation also carried over from lithium to sodium electrolytes with only a simple alignment step.

From there I took two more steps. Reverse design starts from the properties you want and looks for recipes that land there. I also tried trajectory generation, rolling the movie forward with GRU, TCN and causal-transformer models, though I won’t go into that here.

Inside the snapshot encoder

Snapshot encoder

The snapshot encoder is where the physics goes into the architecture, the same way rotation did in Part 1. Each frame becomes a periodic atom graph, and equivariant message passing turns it into 128 learned numbers plus 8 geometric ones, such as lithium coordination and ion contacts: 136 numbers per frame.

Every atom connects to neighbors within 6 Å, using the minimum-image rule across the box boundaries (the box wraps around like Pac-Man), and whole molecules are kept intact instead of getting sliced at the edge. Each atom then carries two kinds of luggage: plain numbers (scalars) and little arrows (vectors). Messages are built from distances and directions, so when you rotate the box, the arrows rotate right along with it and the final pooled numbers don’t change at all. The model doesn’t waste effort learning that a rotated liquid is the same liquid (the same “atom is atom” spirit as Part 1), while still keeping directional information like which way a solvent faces a lithium ion.

Deep dive: the unglamorous speedups

The unglamorous part made everything else possible. Neighbor search went from O(N²) to O(N): instead of every atom asking every other atom “are you close?”, each atom only checks its own neighborhood. Then I froze the encoder and cached about 192 million snapshots once, which took 395 H200 GPU-hours and a cache of about 52 GB. After that, a training step went from 12.6 s to 0.15 s. That’s the difference between “let’s try an idea” and “let’s try an idea next week.”
